title: MIRAGE: Channel-Wise Decomposition for Efficient Image Restoration
one_liner: Assign each part of a neural network to its best job: convolutions fix textures, attention handles distant patterns, and MLPs tune channel statistics.
lead: When a photo is corrupted by noise, blur, or rain, restoring it to clarity takes a lot of computation. Today's best models throw many architectural tools at every part of the problem. MIRAGE notices that these tools have superpowers in different areas: convolutions naturally see nearby pixels (good for texture), attention mechanisms naturally see the whole image at once (good for large structures), and MLPs naturally balance all channels together (good for statistics). By deliberately splitting the work among them, MIRAGE restores images faster, because each tool does only its specialty instead of wasting power on jobs it is bad at, and better, because the model learns more consistent concepts across all depths instead of shallow and deep layers disagreeing.

paras: Image restoration must fix many kinds of damage: noise (random speckles), blur (soft edges), rain streaks, compression artifacts (blocky distortions from file size limits), and mixed combinations. A beginner might train a separate model for each type, but that is wasteful—maintaining five models is expensive.

So researchers built unified models that handle all corruptions at once. But here is the catch: restoring noise needs a model that is sensitive to tiny details in nearby pixels, while restoring blur needs a model that links distant pixels to infer large structures. These two needs pull the architecture in different directions, so unifying them forces the model to compromise—wasting computation on tools it does not need for each specific corruption.

callout.html: MIRAGE gives each architectural piece its best job instead of asking all pieces to do everything.

panels.title: 1. The old way: everything does everything
panels.caption: All modules (conv, attention, MLP) run on all pixels and all channels.

panels.title: 2. The redundancy problem
panels.viz_args: 60% of attention capacity unused for noise; same for conv on global blur.
panels.caption: Each tool carries unused capacity when doing jobs it is not naturally good at.

panels.title: 3. MIRAGE's split
panels.caption: Conv gets texture channels, attention gets global, MLP tunes statistics.

panels.title: 4. Shallow-to-deep consistency
panels.viz_args: Early layers learn texture details; deep layers learn shared structure.
panels.caption: Both depths learn to recognize the same concepts in their own numerical language.

panels.title: 5. The result: small and sharp
panels.caption: Fewer numbers to store, each one working in its assigned specialty.

steps.text: Divide the numbers flowing through the network into three batches: one for convolution, one for attention, one for MLP.

steps.b: Route each group to its natural job
steps.text: Convolution processes its group using local neighborhood rules; attention processes its group by comparing every position to every other; MLP processes its group by mixing all channels together.
Merge the three outputs back into a single result and pass it to the next layer.

steps.b: Measure the learning pattern across depths
steps.text: After the shallow layers learn texture details and the deep layers learn semantic structure, align them in a special space using a contrastive loss.

steps.b: Train end-to-end with fewer numbers to store
steps.text: Each module runs only on the channels it is good at, not all channels, because each tool concentrates on its specialty. The total size shrinks because there are fewer total computations, and restoring a new image runs faster because the model uses less memory and arithmetic.

paras: MIRAGE changes how the channel dimension (the list of numbers describing each pixel position) is split and routed. Instead of passing all channels through all architectural modules, it splits the channels into three disjoint subsets and assigns each subset to exactly one type of module. This is a routing decision: which channels feed into which computational path.

hidden.name: How well shallow and deep layers encode the same patterns
paras: As information flows through a neural network, early layers pick up fine details (like whether a pixel is noisy), while later layers recognize abstract structure (like whether a region is an edge or a flat area). But are they both learning the same thing in their own languages? MIRAGE measures representational alignment—how much the numerical representations from early layers and deep layers actually point to the same concepts, even though they use different numbers.

The paper estimates this by taking the numerical representations from shallow and deep layers, mapping them into a special mathematical space where similarities are measured consistently, and then computing how close the shallow and deep representations cluster. A contrastive loss pushes representations of the same corruption type to stay close and pulls representations of different types apart, which forces the network to learn consistent concepts across all depths.

heat.caption: Darker (higher numbers) means higher alignment between shallow and deep representations at that layer.

reads.html: Shallow layers capture the surface texture of damage; deep layers capture the overall image structure. If both learn to see the same underlying facts about the image, the network avoids learning two conflicting worldviews and generalizes better to corruptions it has never seen, because the abstract understanding is consistent across all parts of the network, not just the top layers.

The paper performs cross-layer contrastive alignment in a special mathematical space (symmetric positive definite), using a contrastive loss to pull similar concepts close together and push different corruption types apart.

mechanism.h2: Why the method works: alignment of strengths
paras: Convolutional filters naturally see only nearby pixels because they use small kernels (typically 3x3). This is a superpower for texture: they instantly capture local patterns. Attention mechanisms compute how every pixel relates to every other pixel, which is expensive but perfect for detecting global structures like large edges or color shifts. MLPs apply the same transformation to each channel independently, which is ideal for balancing channel statistics (how bright or colorful overall).

MIRAGE works because it aligns the architecture with the problem: assigning convolutions to texture channels, attention to structure channels, and MLPs to statistic channels means each module uses only the computational power it needs. This cuts waste and forces the model to use its capacity efficiently. The redundancy that used to be wasted (a convolution over-engineered for global patterns) is eliminated.

The second mechanism is representational alignment. Shallow layers learn corruption-specific textures very quickly, but deep layers learn abstract patterns slowly. Without a tether, they can drift apart and learn conflicting information. By enforcing that the same concepts appear (in different forms) at both depths, the network is forced to build a single consistent world model instead of two separate ones. This consistency transfers to unseen corruptions because the shared abstract understanding generalizes.

stages.s: split channels into texture, structure, statistics groups
route texture group through convolution (local pixel patterns)
route structure group through attention (long-range relationships)
route statistics group through MLP (channel balancing)
merge outputs and measure alignment of shallow and deep representations

math.words: total loss equals reconstruction loss plus weighted Fourier frequency loss plus weighted contrastive alignment loss
math.equation: L_total = L_1 + lambda_f * L_Fourier + lambda_c * L_SPD
symbols: pixel-by-pixel difference between restored and true image
difference in frequency patterns (captures blur and sharpness)
contrastive alignment loss in symmetric positive definite space
weight controlling how much to care about frequency accuracy
weight controlling how much to enforce representational alignment

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model restores a 4-pixel region. L_1 loss: each pixel differs by 1 unit from truth; sum is 4.
L_Fourier loss: the frequency of the blurry region differs by 0.5 units; scaled by lambda_f=0.3 gives 0.15.
L_SPD loss: shallow layer encodes 'this is noise', deep layer encodes 'this is noise but in abstract terms'; they should cluster close in SPD space; penalty is 0.8, scaled by lambda_c=0.5 gives 0.4.
Total: 4 + 0.15 + 0.4 = 4.55. Training nudges the weights to lower this total.

math.note: The three terms enforce that restored pixels match the truth, restored frequencies are sharp, and shallow-deep layers agree on what they see.

charts.title: Generic multi-purpose model
charts.note: All modules run on all channels, wasting capacity because each tool is forced to do jobs it is not designed for, so the model is large. Shallow and deep layers learn conflicting concepts because they are never synchronized, so the model struggles when facing unfamiliar corruption types.

charts.title: MIRAGE (tiny variant)
charts.note: Specialized routing eliminates wasted capacity because each tool only handles what it is good at, making the model four times smaller. Consistent concepts across depths improve generalization because shallow and deep layers share a unified world model, so the model restores better on unfamiliar corruption types.

items.html: If the split of channels into groups is wrong for a new corruption type, the model cannot adapt. A texture-heavy corruption sent to an attention-only branch will perform poorly. The paper assumes the kinds of corruption are known or similar to training data.

If the contrastive loss is too strong, shallow and deep layers become so similar that the network loses the ability to learn progressively more abstract concepts. The model becomes less flexible. Lambda_c must be tuned carefully.

Computing the contrastive alignment loss requires special mathematical operations that can be slower than standard calculations. For real-time applications, this computational overhead must be weighed against the gains in model size.

MIRAGE works best when the correlation between corruption type and representational needs is strong, and when the contrastive weighting balances efficiency and consistency. The method succeeds because the architectural superpowers (convolution for texture, attention for structure, MLP for channel mixing) genuinely exist and are well-matched to image restoration.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny restoration model (under 10 million parameters) that takes as input: a corrupted image, and a label indicating the corruption type (noise, blur, rain, etc.). Split its channels as MIRAGE does. Train on a mix of corruptions. Then test on a new image with a corruption type the model has seen before (in-distribution), and then on a real-world photo with mixed corruption the model has never encountered (zero-shot).
demo.closing: The demo succeeds if the MIRAGE model (tiny) outperforms a generic model (large) on zero-shot generalization, proving that specialization via channel routing (because each tool does its best job) and representational alignment (because all layers share a consistent world model) actually transfer to new corruptions.
